sentences.text: Iro is thirty-nine.
She works for the port authority and she dives most weekends and the ledge at Agriolivado is still there.
The shelves are still there.
Some of the things have changed.

The mannequin's arm turned up on the fourth shelf about eleven years ago, which she took personally and which she has never mentioned to her uncle, who is seventy-six and who has not been over the side of a boat since 2009 and who still says *over* about anything that is not a fish.
She has had a long time to think about it and she has three positions, and she holds all three at once, which she has stopped apologising for.
The first is her uncle's and it is almost certainly correct.
Octopuses collect.
They are extremely clever and they manipulate objects constantly and they arrange the things round a den.
Any pattern she has found in eight cracks in a rock is a pattern she has brought with her, and a person who dives the same ledge for thirty years will find whatever they went down for.
This position is dull and well supported and she has never been able to knock it over.
The second is that the order is real.
She has photographs.
She has, in a folder, six hundred pictures of those eight shelves taken over twenty years, and the categories hold.
Things have moved shelf — the broken camera was on the edges shelf for a season and then was not — and every move she has recorded has been in the direction of a better fit, never a worse one.
The third is the one she does not say out loud very often.
She said it once, at a conference in Heraklion, to a marine biologist she had been talking to for about an hour and who had been extremely interested up to that point.
The conversation ended shortly afterwards in a friendly way and the woman was perfectly nice about it.
Iro does not blame her and would probably have done the same.
It is that the shelves are not for the octopus.
Everything about them is arranged for something with eyes at the height of that ledge, that swims past, that understands what a cup is.
There is exactly one animal in that sea that fits, and it is the animal that has been throwing things over the side of boats off Panormos since before anybody kept records.
Somebody down there has been sorting our rubbish for a very long time, by what we made it for, and putting it out along a face where we would find it.
Iro has never taken anything off those shelves.

She took the compass back once, in 2011, having found a second one in a junk shop in Kalymnos — the same pattern, the glass intact — and she put it on the ledge at the end of the second shelf, and came up, and went home.
It was on the shelf, in the row, in the right place, the following weekend.
It has been there fourteen years and it has never moved, and she checks every time, and she has never worked out whether that means it was accepted or whether it means nothing at all.
